unit.title: The human body
unit.blurb: How your heart, blood, lungs and body systems keep you alive – and how we keep healthy.

O1.t: Describe the parts of the circulatory system (heart, blood vessels and blood) and what each part does.

O2.t: Measure pulse rate, record the results in a table and say how exercise changes pulse rate.

O3.t: Describe the parts of the respiratory system and how we breathe in and breathe out.

O4.t: Explain why we breathe, use a model of the lungs and read a line graph of breathing rate.

O5.t: Describe the body changes of puberty and name the main parts of the reproductive system.

O6.t: Name living things that cause disease and describe how the body defends itself.

O7.t: Describe how hygiene, clean water and avoiding insect bites stop diseases spreading.

captions: Hello, scientists! Welcome to Atomic Science, Stage 6.
This is lesson 1.1: the circulatory system.
Put your hand on your chest, a little to the left.
Can you feel a soft beat, again and again?
That is your heart. It is working all day and all night, even when you are asleep.
Your heart is part of the circulatory system.
It has three main parts.
The heart.
The blood vessels.
And the blood.
Together, they carry food and oxygen to every part of your body, and they carry waste away.
Make a fist. Your heart is about the same size as your fist.
It sits inside your chest, behind your ribs.
The ribs are like a strong cage that protects it.
Your heart is a special muscle, and its job is to pump.
Look at this water pump. When we squeeze it, water is pushed along the pipe.
Your heart works in the same way. Each time the heart muscle squeezes, it pushes blood along.
We call each squeeze a heartbeat.
The heart has two sides.
The right side pumps blood to the lungs, where the blood picks up oxygen.
The left side pumps this oxygen-rich blood all around the body.
Here is a tip: on a heart drawing, the sides are swapped, because you are looking at someone facing you.
Time to think! Which side of the heart pumps blood to the lungs?
Blood is a red liquid that flows around your body.
It carries food and oxygen to all your body parts.
On the way back, it picks up waste, such as carbon dioxide.
Carbon dioxide is a waste gas. Your lungs get rid of it when you breathe out.
Blood travels in tubes called blood vessels. There are three kinds.
Arteries carry blood away from the heart. They have thick, stretchy walls, because the blood inside is pushed hard.
Veins carry blood back to the heart. Their walls are thinner.
Capillaries are tiny. They join arteries to veins, and their walls are so thin that oxygen and food can pass through them into the body.
Let's follow the blood on its journey.
The heart pumps blood to the lungs. There, the blood picks up oxygen.
The blood comes back to the heart.
Then the heart pumps it out to the rest of the body, where the oxygen is used.
Finally, the blood returns to the heart, and the journey starts again. It never stops!
Pause and think. Can you put the journey of the blood in the right order?
Many other animals with a backbone have a circulatory system like ours.
A fish, a frog and a bird all have a heart, blood vessels and blood.
A fish's heart sends blood to its gills to collect oxygen from the water.
Each time your heart beats, it pushes blood into your arteries with pressure.
You can feel this push in your wrist, or at the side of your neck. This is your pulse.
Use two fingers, not your thumb, because your thumb has its own pulse.
Now let's be scientists and measure our pulse rate.
Find your pulse and start a timer.
Count the beats for one minute. That number is your pulse rate, in beats per minute.
Do it three times, write each result in a table, and work out the average.
What happens after exercise? Here are one learner's results.
Sitting still, her pulse rate was about 85 beats per minute.
After walking, it went up. After running, it went up even more.
When we exercise, our muscles need more food and oxygen, so the heart beats faster to deliver it.
Your turn! Why does the heart beat faster when we run?
Let's remember what we learned.
The heart is a muscle that pumps blood.
Arteries, veins and capillaries carry the blood.
Blood carries food and oxygen, and takes away carbon dioxide.
And your pulse rate goes up when you exercise.
Great work! Now go to the practice room to listen to and say the new words.

captions: Welcome back, scientists!
This is lesson 1.2: the respiratory system.
Put your hands on your ribs and take a deep breath in.
Can you feel your chest getting bigger?
Now breathe out slowly. Your chest gets smaller again.
You do this about sixteen times every minute, without even thinking about it!
The respiratory system is the body system we use for breathing.
It has two lungs.
It has air tubes, such as the windpipe, that lead from your nose and mouth to the lungs.
And it has muscles that move air in and out.
Your lungs are in your chest, protected by your ribs.
They are soft and stretchy, a bit like sponges that fill up with air.
Let's look at breathing in.
The diaphragm is a sheet of muscle under the lungs. It tightens and moves down.
The ribs move up and out.
The chest gets bigger, so air rushes in through the nose or mouth, down the windpipe, and into the lungs.
Now breathing out.
The diaphragm relaxes and moves back up.
The ribs move down and in.
The chest gets smaller, so air is pushed out of the lungs.
Stop and think. What does the diaphragm do when we breathe in?
Why do we breathe? We need oxygen to stay alive.
In the lungs, oxygen moves from the air into tiny blood vessels.
The blood carries the oxygen to the heart, and then all around the body.
Your body makes carbon dioxide as waste. The blood brings it back to the lungs, and we breathe it out.
Scientists use models to explain things we cannot see.
In this model, the bottle is the chest, and the balloon inside is a lung.
The straw is the windpipe, and the stretchy sheet at the bottom is the diaphragm.
Pull the sheet down, and the balloon fills with air. Let it go back up, and the air is pushed out. Just like breathing!
Pause here. In the model, which part acts like the diaphragm?
Breathing rate is the number of breaths you take in one minute.
Let's investigate how exercise changes it.
Count your breaths at rest. Then run on the spot for two minutes, and count again.
Keep measuring every two minutes while you rest.
We can show the results on a line graph.
The breathing rate goes up during exercise, because the body needs more oxygen.
When we rest, it slowly comes back down to normal.
From this graph, it takes about six minutes to get back to normal.
Now look at the graph. What was the breathing rate just after running?
Let's remember.
We breathe using our lungs, the windpipe and our chest muscles.
When we breathe in, the diaphragm moves down and the ribs move up and out.
When we breathe out, the diaphragm moves up and the ribs move down and in.
And exercise makes our breathing rate go up.
Well done! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.

captions: Hello again, scientists!
This is lesson 1.3: growing up, and the reproductive system.
Every living thing has a life cycle.
A baby grows into a child. A child grows into a teenager, and then into an adult.
Adults can have babies of their own. Making new living things is called reproduction.
Without reproduction, a kind of living thing would die out.
As a child, you grow taller and heavier every year.
Then there is a special time when your body changes from a child's body into an adult's body.
This time is called puberty.
Puberty usually starts at about eleven in girls, and a little later in boys. Everyone is different, and that is normal.
The changes are caused by chemical messengers in the body, called hormones.
First, you may have a growth spurt, and grow ten centimetres or more in a year.
More hair grows, and the skin can become oily, so some people get spots.
Voices get deeper, especially in boys.
And the body shape changes: shoulders get broader in boys, and hips get wider in girls.
Quick check. What causes the body changes in puberty?
Puberty also brings changes inside the body, in the reproductive system.
The main job of the reproductive system is to make special cells for reproduction, called sex cells.
The male sex cells are called sperm. The female sex cells are called eggs, or ova.
Sperm cells have a tail, so they can swim. An egg cell is much bigger, and it cannot move by itself.
When a sperm cell joins with an egg cell, a new life begins.
This joining is called fertilisation.
The fertilised egg grows into a baby inside the mother's uterus, also called the womb.
In males, two testes make the sperm, and the sperm duct carries it.
In females, two ovaries make the eggs.
Fertilisation happens in a tube called the oviduct.
And the baby grows in the uterus.
Think about it. Where in the female body does fertilisation take place?
About a year after puberty starts, girls begin to have periods. This is called menstruation.
About once a month, an egg that has not been fertilised leaves the body, together with the lining of the uterus.
This causes some bleeding for a few days. It is a normal and healthy part of growing up.
Let's remember.
Reproduction makes new living things.
Puberty is the time when a child's body changes into an adult's body.
Hormones cause the changes of puberty.
And when a sperm and an egg join, we call it fertilisation.
Great job! If you have questions about growing up, talk to a parent or a teacher you trust.

captions: Hello, scientists!
This is lesson 1.4: diseases, and how we can stop them spreading.
Have you ever had a cold, or chicken pox?
A disease stops our body from working properly.
Some diseases are infectious. This means they can be passed from one person to another.
Many diseases are caused by tiny living things.
A living thing that lives on or inside another living thing, and harms it, is called a parasite.
The living thing it lives on is called the host.
Bacteria are very small. We need a microscope to see them. Some bacteria cause diseases such as cholera, but many bacteria are harmless.
Viruses are even smaller than bacteria. They cause flu, measles and chicken pox.
Some fungi are parasites too. They cause athlete's foot and ringworm.
Other parasites cause diseases like malaria.
Pause and think. Which is the smallest: a bacterium, a virus, or a fungus?
Germs are all around us. So why are we not ill all the time?
Our body has defences.
The skin is a barrier that stops germs getting in.
Tears contain a chemical that kills some bacteria.
Sticky mucus in the nose and windpipe traps germs.
And acid in the stomach kills germs in our food.
We can help to stop diseases from spreading with good hygiene. This means keeping ourselves and our things clean.
Wash your hands with soap and water before you eat, and after you use the toilet.
Soap helps to remove germs that water alone leaves behind.
Then dry your hands on a clean towel.
When you sneeze, tiny drops spray into the air, and they can carry germs.
So cover your nose and mouth with a tissue, or sneeze into your elbow, not your hand.
Also, drink only clean, safe water, keep food covered, and keep kitchens and toilets clean.
Your turn. Why should we wash our hands with soap, and not just with water?
Some insects spread diseases. Mosquitoes can spread malaria.
The mosquito does not get ill itself. It carries the parasite from one person to another. We call it a vector.
To avoid bites, sleep under a bed net, wear long sleeves, and use insect repellent.
Here is a safe experiment you can try.
Use glitter as pretend germs on your hands.
Try washing in different ways: water only, and then soap and water.
Count how much glitter is left each time. Which way removes the most germs?
Let's remember.
Bacteria, viruses, some fungi and other parasites can cause disease.
Our skin, tears, mucus and stomach acid help to defend us.
Good hygiene stops diseases from spreading.
And bed nets and repellent help to stop insect bites.
Fantastic work, scientists! See you in the practice room.
